stem: The family of an eight-year-old child drives to a hospital so the child can receive chemotherapy for acute leukemia. The child begins to develop nausea and vomits every time they visit the hospital for repeat chemotherapy. According to learning theory, this is an example of:
explanation_text:
Classical vs. Operant Conditioning Classical conditioning: a neutral cue is repeatedly paired with something that already triggers an automatic reflex, until the cue alone produces the response. Here the hospital (neutral) is paired with chemo (causes nausea), so eventually the hospital alone triggers nausea — anticipatory nausea.
Operant conditioning is different: a voluntary behavior is shaped by its consequences (reward or punishment).
Quick check: reflex triggered by a paired cue = classical; voluntary behavior changed by its consequences = operant.

An overweight teenager is seen for headache and visual disturbance. She describes the headache as 4/1O pain intensity over her entire head and worse with coughing and sneezing. She has been noticing worsening of vision described as periods of blurring and darkening of vision. MRI of the brain is normal. Which of the following would confirm the suspected diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri) Classic picture: an overweight young woman with headache, papilledema, and visual changes — but a NORMAL brain MRI (no mass, no hydrocephalus).
The problem is raised intracranial pressure with no structural cause. A lumbar puncture confirms it (high opening pressure) and can also relieve symptoms.
Real-world clue: high-pressure signs (headache worse with coughing or straining, transient vision loss) plus normal imaging. Untreated it can cause permanent vision loss. Linked to obesity, vitamin A, and tetracyclines.

A 43-year-old patient with newly diagnosed acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) has increasing social withdrawal and irritability over several weeks. The patient has not been able to remember phone numbers, has not been doing household chores, and appears distracted. Motor examination reveals mild right hemiparesis, left limb ataxia, and bilateral visual field defects. A lumbar puncture reveals normal cell counts, protein, and glucose. A T2 weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of this patient is shown in the figure. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
PML: JC Virus in Severe Immunosuppression PML = reactivation of the JC virus, which destroys oligodendrocytes (the myelin-making cells) in severely immunosuppressed patients — classically advanced AIDS.
This produces multifocal, asymmetric white-matter lesions and matching deficits (hemiparesis, ataxia, visual-field cuts) that worsen over weeks. The CSF is typically bland — normal cells, protein, and glucose, as seen here.
Memory hook: “multifocal” = scattered white-matter lesions on MRI in an immunocompromised patient, with no mass effect.

A patient has ambiguous results on a multiple sleep latency test. Which of the following would confirm the suspected diagnosis of narcolepsy?
explanation_text:
Narcolepsy: Low CSF Orexin (Hypocretin) Narcolepsy (type 1) is caused by loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the hypothalamus — the signal that keeps you awake and stabilizes the sleep–wake switch. Without it, REM sleep intrudes into wakefulness (cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations).
When the multiple sleep latency test is ambiguous, a low CSF orexin level confirms the diagnosis.
Real-world hook: orexin is the brain’s “wakefulness fuel.” Low fuel = sudden sleep attacks and REM leaking into the day.

During a therapy session with a patient, the therapist coughs while the patient is speaking. The patient angrily states, "If you disagree with me just tell me, but don't be a passive aggressive jerk!" In the ensuing discussion, the therapist shares the interpretation that the patient is consistently treating the therapist like an aggressor. Which of the following modalities of therapy best classifies this therapy session?

options.text: Systems training for emotional predictability and problem solving

explanation_text:
Transference: Reliving Old Relationships in Therapy Transference = a patient unconsciously redirecting feelings from important past relationships onto the therapist. Here the patient experiences a harmless cough as an attack, treating the therapist as an “aggressor.”
Transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP), developed for borderline personality disorder, deliberately uses these in-session reactions to help the patient recognize and integrate distorted views of self and others.
Contrast: CBT targets thoughts, DBT builds emotion-regulation skills, while TFP works the therapy relationship itself.

Which of the following circuits mediates the ability to resist responding to aggravating situations with hostility?
explanation_text:
Prefrontal Circuits: The Orbitofrontal “Brakes” The orbitofrontal cortex is the brain’s impulse-control “brake” — it lets you resist reacting to provocation with hostility. Damage here causes disinhibition, impulsivity, and aggression (the classic Phineas Gage personality change).
The three classic prefrontal circuits: dorsolateral = executive function and planning; orbitofrontal = social inhibition and impulse control; anterior cingulate = motivation and initiation (apathy when damaged).
Real-world hook: the orbitofrontal cortex is the filter sitting between an aggravating situation and your reaction.

Evidence on both examinations of affective !ability that is situationally dependent

answer_text: Logical and coherent speech on the first examination but disorganized speech on the second
answer_raw: E. Logical and coherent speech on the first examination but disorganized speech on the second
explanation_text:
Delirium: Acute, Fluctuating, Inattentive The hallmark of delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that fluctuates over hours — which is why this patient is coherent at one exam and disorganized at the next.
Contrast with dementia, which is gradual and stable (a consistently low MMSE alone does not indicate delirium). Delirium waxes and wanes and almost always has an underlying medical cause (infection, medications, metabolic upset).
Real-world hook: waxing-and-waning confusion with inattention = delirium until proven otherwise — hunt for the medical trigger.

stem: Feelings of persecution are most reflective of which of the following defense mechanisms?
explanation_text:
Defense Mechanisms: Projection Projection = unconsciously attributing your own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else. A hostile person “sees” hostility in others and feels persecuted — the threat feels external instead of internal.
Quick contrasts: denial = refusing to accept reality; repression = unconsciously blocking a memory or impulse; reaction formation = acting the opposite of how you feel; regression = reverting to earlier, childlike behavior under stress.
Real-world hook: persecutory or paranoid feelings (“everyone is out to get me”) classically point to projection.

An 84-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with fever, dry mouth, and visual hallucinations. The patient is tachycardic and restless. The toxicity of which of the following medications is most likely to explain the patient's symptoms?
explanation_text:
Anticholinergic Toxicity (Benztropine) Benztropine blocks acetylcholine, so its toxicity is the classic anticholinergic toxidrome. Mnemonic: “hot as a hare (fever), dry as a bone (no sweat or saliva), red as a beet (flushed), blind as a bat (dilated pupils), mad as a hatter (delirium, hallucinations)” — plus tachycardia and urinary retention.
This is the mirror image of cholinergic excess (the wet “SLUDGE” picture).
Real-world hook: elderly + fever + dry mouth + visual hallucinations + tachycardia = anticholinergic toxicity. Other common culprits: TCAs, diphenhydramine, oxybutynin.

During an initial appointment, a 23-year-old patient reports frequently engaging in shopping sprees and binge eating. The patient cycles through moods quickly, sometimes as frequently as hourly. Within the first ten minutes of the visit, the patient voices appreciation that the intake doctor is "the only one" who has ever genuinely listened, sharing that everyone else has stopped visiting. What is the patient's most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Borderline Personality Disorder & Splitting Core features: mood that shifts within hours, impulsivity (shopping sprees, binge eating), stormy relationships, and a fragile sense of self. The key clue here is splitting — idealizing the new doctor as the “only one” who understands while devaluing everyone else.
Distinguish from bipolar: borderline mood swings are rapid (minutes to hours) and triggered by interpersonal events; bipolar episodes last days to weeks and are more autonomous.
Real-world hook: rapid idealize-then-devalue (“splitting”) + chronic emptiness + fear of abandonment = borderline.

A patient presents with acute onset of pain and decreased vision in the right eye. The patient reports that colors look faded when viewed through the right eye. On examination, the patient is noted to have a right afferent pupillary defect and a swollen right optic disc. The patient spontaneously recovers over the next six weeks. Which of the following disorders is the patient most likely to later develop?
explanation_text:
Optic Neuritis: A Red Flag for MS This is optic neuritis: acute painful vision loss in one eye, an afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil), washed-out color vision (especially red), and a swollen optic disc — usually recovering over weeks.
It is often the first demyelinating attack of multiple sclerosis. MS is diagnosed when CNS lesions are disseminated in space and time (different sites, different times).
Real-world hook: young adult + painful one-eye vision loss + faded colors + afferent pupillary defect = optic neuritis — screen for MS with a brain MRI.

Prolonged stimulation of N-methyl-D-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptors is hypothesized to result in neuronal death due to:

options.text: Excessive calcium influx resulting in mitochondrial caspase activation
Reduced sodium influx resulting in relative hypotonicity and cellular necrosis
Excessive chloride influx resulting in relative hypertonicity and cellular necrosis
Increased ATP production resulting in collapse of sodium and potassium gradients
Increased production of beta-amyloid resulting in disruption of the cellular cytoskeleton

answer_text: Excessive calcium influx resulting in mitochondrial caspase activation
answer_raw: A. Excessive calcium influx resulting in mitochondrial caspase activation
explanation_text:
Excitotoxicity: Calcium Is the Culprit NMDA receptors let calcium into neurons. Brief activation is normal and vital for learning, but prolonged overstimulation (by glutamate during stroke, seizure, or injury) floods the cell with calcium.
That calcium overload switches on destructive enzymes and triggers mitochondrial caspase activation — programmed cell death (apoptosis). This process is called excitotoxicity.
Real-world hook: calcium is the toxic messenger. This is why NMDA modulators like memantine and ketamine act on this pathway.

When upset, the child does not seek comfort from the caregiver. The child has episodes of unexplained irritability and sadness. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis for this child?
explanation_text:
Reactive Attachment Disorder vs. DSED Reactive attachment disorder follows grossly inadequate caregiving (neglect, repeated foster placements), so the child never forms a secure attachment. The child is emotionally withdrawn — rarely seeks or responds to comfort, shows little positive affect, and has unexplained irritability or sadness.
Contrast with disinhibited social engagement disorder (DSED): same neglect history, but the child is overly familiar and approaches strangers without caution.
Real-world hook: same root cause (early neglect), opposite social style — RAD = withdrawn and inhibited; DSED = indiscriminately friendly.

A patient and spouse report that the patient has been having vivid dreams, acting them out during sleep by kicking, swearing and even punching the spouse while asleep and dreaming. Which diagnosis is frequently preceded by the development of this sleep disorder?
explanation_text:
REM Sleep Behavior Disorder → Parkinson Normally REM sleep paralyzes your muscles so you cannot act out dreams. In REM sleep behavior disorder that paralysis fails, so the person physically acts out vivid dreams — kicking, punching, yelling.
This disorder is a strong early warning sign of synucleinopathies, especially Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia, often appearing years before motor symptoms.
Real-world hook: an older adult who acts out dreams and injures a bed partner = think future Parkinson or Lewy body disease. Confirm with polysomnography.

After a stroke, a patient does not recognize his wife, believing that the person in front of him is a double who is impersonating her. He acknowledges that she looks like his wife, but he feels no emotional connection to her. From a learning theory perspective, which of the following processing errors leads to the delusional conviction?
explanation_text:
Capgras Delusion (Misidentification) Capgras delusion = believing a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor. The patient recognizes the face but feels no emotional familiarity, so the brain “explains” the mismatch by deciding it must be a double.
In learning-theory terms this is a prediction error: the expected emotional response to a loved one’s face never arrives, and the false belief resolves the conflict. It often follows a stroke that disconnects face recognition from emotional centers.
Real-world hook: “looks like her but isn’t her” = Capgras. (Fregoli is the opposite — strangers seen as one familiar person in disguise.)

stem: Which of the following structures has a direct connection to the amygdala and is involved in the neural processing of pain signals from the peripheral nervous system?
answer_text: Periaqueductal gray E. Parabrachial nucleus of the pons
answer_raw: B. Periaqueductal gray E. Parabrachial nucleus of the pons
explanation_text:
Periaqueductal Gray: The Pain Volume Knob The periaqueductal gray (PAG) is the brain’s master switch for descending pain control. It links to the amygdala (the emotional weight of pain) and drives pathways through the rostroventral medulla to the spinal cord that dampen incoming pain signals.
This is where opioids and stress-induced analgesia act — stimulating the PAG powerfully suppresses pain.
Real-world hook: the PAG is the “volume knob” that turns pain down; the parabrachial nucleus relays pain up to the amygdala, giving pain its emotional alarm.

First-Line for GAD: SSRI/SNRI, Not Benzos First-line drug therapy for generalized anxiety disorder is an SSRI or SNRI. They treat the chronic anxiety effectively and are not addictive.
Benzodiazepines act fast but are avoided here because of the patient’s frequent alcohol use — both are CNS depressants (additive sedation and respiratory risk) and carry dependence and abuse potential.

Enhancement of dopamine transmission in which of the following tracts is associated with the addicting and reinforcing effects of repeated exposure to psychostimulant drugs of abuse?
explanation_text:
Dopamine Tracts: Mesolimbic = Reward The mesolimbic pathway (ventral tegmental area → nucleus accumbens) is the brain’s reward circuit. Drugs of abuse converge here by boosting dopamine, which drives the “high” and reinforces repeated use.
The four dopamine tracts: mesolimbic = reward/addiction (and positive psychotic symptoms); mesocortical = cognition/negative symptoms; nigrostriatal = movement (Parkinson, EPS); tuberoinfundibular = prolactin (block it → high prolactin).
Real-world hook: mesolimbic = “want it again” — the final common pathway of addiction.

A 72-year-old woman presents with acute headache and an inability to read. Additional testing reveals that the woman is unable to write fluently but her verbal fluency is intact. Thrombosis of which of the following arteries would result in this syndrome?
explanation_text:
Alexia Without Agraphia (Left PCA Stroke) A left posterior cerebral artery stroke damages the left visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum. The patient still sees and writes, but visual word information from the intact right visual cortex cannot cross to the left-hemisphere language areas.
Result: she can write a sentence but cannot read it back — “word blindness” with preserved writing and speech.
Real-world hook: writes fine but cannot read = alexia without agraphia, classically a left PCA stroke (often with a right visual-field cut).

stem: Disequilibrium elicited while standing with feet together and eyes closed usually indicates a disorder of:
explanation_text:
Romberg Sign = Proprioception Loss Staying upright needs two of three inputs: vision, vestibular sense, and proprioception (joint-position sense carried by the dorsal columns). A positive Romberg = steady with eyes open but swaying when they close, so proprioception is the failing input (vision had been compensating).
This localizes to the posterior (dorsal) spinal columns — e.g., B12 deficiency or tabes dorsalis. Cerebellar disease causes imbalance even with eyes open (a negative Romberg).
Real-world hook: falls only when the eyes close = sensory (dorsal-column) ataxia, not cerebellar.

answer_raw: C. Continuous suicidal ideation with a plan
explanation_text:
When to Choose ECT: Need for Speed ECT is the fastest, most effective treatment for severe depression — used when you cannot wait for medications or they have already failed. Its strongest indications are acute dangers: active suicidal ideation with a plan, refusal to eat or drink, or catatonia.
In pregnancy ECT is relatively safe and is preferred over a long medication trial when the situation is urgent. The other options here are ordinary depressive symptoms, not emergencies.
Real-world hook: ECT = “we need this person better now” — active suicidality, catatonia, or food refusal.

stem: A local organization is providing naloxone education and access in areas with higher prevalence of opiate use disorders. Which of the following best describes this intervention?

Harm Reduction vs. Prevention Harm reduction accepts that drug use is happening and aims to reduce its dangers without requiring abstinence. Distributing naloxone (the opioid-overdose reversal drug) so people can survive an overdose is a classic example — along with needle exchanges and safe-use sites.
Contrast: primary prevention stops a problem before it starts; medication-assisted treatment (methadone, buprenorphine) treats the addiction itself.
Real-world hook: harm reduction = keep people alive and safer now, whether or not they are ready to quit.

Types of Memory Long-term memory splits into declarative (conscious “knowing that”) and implicit/procedural (“knowing how”). Declarative has two types: semantic = general facts and knowledge (Paris is in France), and episodic = personal experiences tied to a time and place (your last birthday).
Procedural memory = skills you perform automatically (riding a bike); sensory memory is the brief, raw snapshot of incoming stimuli.
Real-world hook: semantic = facts; episodic = events; procedural = skills.

A patient with treatment-resistant depression has a rapid antidepressant response to a single dose of intravenous ketamine. Antagonism of which of the following neurotransmitter systems has been most implicated in this treatment response?
explanation_text:
Ketamine: Rapid Antidepressant via NMDA Ketamine blocks (antagonizes) the NMDA glutamate receptor. This triggers a surge of glutamate signaling and rapid synapse growth (via BDNF), which can lift treatment-resistant depression within hours — far faster than SSRIs, which take weeks.
This is a fundamentally different mechanism from monoamine antidepressants, and it can work even after those have failed.
Real-world hook: ketamine = NMDA antagonist → hours-not-weeks antidepressant effect; the basis for esketamine nasal spray.

A study examines the efficacy of lithium in preventing suicide in patients diagnosed with severe major depressive disorder over a one-year period. A total of 1000 subjects are recruited into the study; 500 are randomized to receive placebo, while 500 are randomized to receive lithium. After one year, a total of 50 subjects in the placebo group commit suicide, compared to 25 subjects in the lithium group. According to this data, what is the number needed to treat with lithium in order to prevent one suicide?
explanation_text:
Number Needed to Treat (NNT) NNT = how many patients you must treat to prevent one bad outcome. The formula is NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction (ARR).
Here: placebo suicide rate = 50/500 = 10%; lithium = 25/500 = 5%. ARR = 10% − 5% = 5% (0.05). NNT = 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20.
Real-world hook: a lower NNT means a more effective treatment. Always build it from the absolute risk difference, not the relative one.

The patient describes their daily activities as "dreamlike" and feeling "robotic" at times. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Depersonalization / Derealization Depersonalization = feeling detached from yourself (“watching someone else live my life,” robotic, numb). Derealization = the world feels unreal or dreamlike. Crucially, reality testing stays intact — the person knows it only feels that way.
It is often triggered by stress or anxiety and is distressing but benign, unlike psychosis (no loss of reality) or dissociative amnesia (memory gaps).
Real-world hook: “I feel unreal but I know I’m not crazy” = depersonalization/derealization; intact insight separates it from psychosis.

stem: Secondary mania is most likely to arise in the setting of which of the following illnesses?
explanation_text:
Secondary Mania (a Medical Cause) “Secondary” mania means manic symptoms caused by a medical or neurological condition rather than bipolar disorder. Multiple sclerosis is a classic cause — demyelinating lesions disrupt the frontal and temporal circuits that regulate mood.
Suspect a secondary cause when mania appears for the first time late in life, has no psychiatric history, or comes with neurologic signs. Other triggers: stroke, steroids, HIV, hyperthyroidism.
Real-world hook: new mania + neuro findings, or a first episode in an older patient = hunt for a medical cause, not just bipolar.

explanation_text:
Clozapine Myocarditis Clozapine can cause myocarditis, usually within the first 4–8 weeks. Clues: new dyspnea, tachycardia, hypotension, chest pain, fever, eosinophilia, and ECG changes. A troponin (with CRP) confirms cardiac injury and guides stopping the drug.

explanation_text:
Effect Size = Magnitude of the Difference Effect size measures how big a difference is in standardized units — roughly the difference in means divided by the standard deviation (Cohen’s d). It answers “how much does the treatment matter?”
Unlike the p-value (which only says whether a difference is statistically real, and shrinks with larger samples), effect size captures the practical magnitude of benefit regardless of sample size.
Real-world hook: p-value = is it real? Effect size = is it big enough to matter? (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.)

stem: A patient has intact somatosensory functioning for light touch, pressure, temperature, pain, vibration, and proprioception. However, the patient is unable to recognize objects based on touch. Which of the following brain regions is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation_text:
Astereognosis: Parietal Association Cortex Primary sensation is intact (touch, pain, temperature, vibration, proprioception all work), yet the patient cannot identify objects by feel. The problem is not the sensation itself but the interpretation of it.
That higher-order integration happens in the posterior parietal (somatosensory association) cortex. Damage there causes tactile agnosia, or astereognosis — raw sensory data arrives but is not recognized.
Real-world hook: feels the key normally but cannot tell it is a key = an association-cortex problem (posterior parietal), not primary sensory loss.

stem: A 15-year-old patient has had an 18-month history of waxing and waning episodes of nonrhythmic and recurrent eye blinking, shoulder shrugging, and facial grimacing. The patient can suppress the movements for short periods, but they get worse when he is tired or anxious. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Tic Disorders: Tourette vs. Persistent Tic Tics are sudden, repetitive, nonrhythmic movements (motor) or sounds (vocal). They are briefly suppressible and worsen with stress or fatigue — exactly as described here.
Diagnose by type and duration: Tourette = both motor AND vocal tics for over a year. Persistent (chronic) tic disorder = only motor OR only vocal tics for over a year. Here there are only motor tics, so it is persistent motor tic disorder.
Contrast: stereotypies are rhythmic and not suppressible; dystonia is sustained twisting postures.

Within a short time, the child develops symptoms of separation anxiety and concern about the health of the surviving parent. The appearance of these new symptoms is most consistent with which of the following?

options.text: Insecure attachment to the deceased parent
Increased risk for the emergence of a major depressive episode
Cognitive distortion that the child is responsible for the parent's death
Inability of the surviving parent to be emotionally available to the child

answer_raw: B. Age-typical presentation of normal bereavement
explanation_text:
Normal Childhood Bereavement After a parent’s death, it is developmentally normal for a child to develop new separation anxiety and worry about the surviving parent’s health. Children’s grief often shows up as clinging, regression, and fears rather than adult-style sadness.
It becomes concerning only if symptoms are severe, prolonged, or impairing — then consider major depression or prolonged grief. Self-blame or “insecure attachment” is not the default interpretation.
Real-world hook: separation fears after losing a parent = expected grief, not pathology; support and watch before diagnosing.

Loss of nicotinic receptor sites and potentiation of remaining receptor sites are processes involved in the pathophysiology of:
explanation_text:
Cholinergic Hypothesis of Alzheimer Disease Alzheimer disease involves loss of acetylcholine-producing neurons (especially from the nucleus basalis of Meynert), with loss of nicotinic receptors. This cholinergic deficit tracks with the memory and attention problems.
That is why cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) help — they raise available acetylcholine and modestly improve symptoms (they do not stop the disease).
Real-world hook: Alzheimer = low acetylcholine → cholinesterase inhibitors; memantine instead targets the glutamate/NMDA system.

answer_raw: E. Cumulative central nervous system depression
explanation_text:
Gabapentin + Opioids: Additive CNS Depression Gabapentin and opioids are both CNS depressants. Combined, they additively suppress breathing and arousal — the FDA warns this raises the risk of respiratory depression, oversedation, and death, especially in older adults or those with lung disease.
Gabapentin is often seen as “benign,” but it has real abuse potential and is dangerous when paired with opioids or other sedatives.
Real-world hook: stacking CNS depressants (opioid + gabapentin + benzo + alcohol) = respiratory depression; the danger is sedation, not the liver.

A 72-year-old woman with no past psychiatric history presents to the emergency department for evaluation of aggression. She is accompanied by her daughter, who states that the patient has been yelling and throwing various items at her home health care nurse for the past week. The patient has not been aggressive towards any family members, and the daughter denies any history of similar episodes. Initial medical workup is unremarkable, and the patient has a Montreal Cognitive Assessment Test (MoCA) score of 26. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her behavior?
explanation_text:
Spotting Elder Abuse The key clue: the aggression targets only the paid caregiver (home-health nurse), not family, with no prior episodes and near-normal cognition (MoCA 26). That pattern argues against delirium or dementia and toward a reaction to mistreatment.
New behavioral changes in an elder aimed at a specific caregiver should raise suspicion for abuse or neglect — consider it before blaming a neurocognitive disorder.
Real-world hook: situational aggression + intact cognition + a specific caregiver = think elder abuse, and screen.

Following gastric bypass surgery, continued abuse of which of the following substances could more readily lead to life-endangering consequences than before surgery?
explanation_text:
Alcohol After Gastric Bypass After Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, alcohol bypasses much of the stomach and empties quickly into the small intestine, so it is absorbed faster, peaks higher, and undergoes less first-pass metabolism. The same drink now causes quicker, stronger intoxication.
Bariatric patients are also at higher risk of developing a new alcohol use disorder, making continued drinking genuinely more dangerous than before surgery.
Real-world hook: post-bypass = less stomach, so faster and higher alcohol levels — easier to get dangerously drunk.

stem: Disruption of cortical areas that form the salience network would most prominently impair functioning in:
explanation_text:
The Salience Network The salience network (anterior insula + dorsal anterior cingulate) is the brain’s “filter” — it constantly scans internal and external input to flag what is important and worth attention, then switches the brain between its internal (default-mode) and task (executive) networks.
Damage impairs detection of relevant or salient stimuli: the person cannot tell what deserves focus.
Real-world hook: the salience network is the “what matters right now?” detector — disrupted in addiction, psychosis, and frontotemporal dementia.

answer_text: Personality change due to another medical condition
answer_raw: E. Personality change due to another medical condition
explanation_text:
Apathy vs. Depression in Neurodegeneration Apathy = loss of motivation, interest, and spontaneity without sadness. The giveaway here: he denies low mood, has no neurovegetative symptoms, and is not distressed by his own anhedonia — that lack of distress points to apathy, not depression.
In Huntington (a frontal-subcortical disease), the brain damage itself produces this change, coded as “personality change due to another medical condition.”
Real-world hook: amotivation and flat interest, but not sad and not bothered by it = apathy from the disease, not major depression.

stem: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) primarily acts by activating which of the following receptors?
explanation_text:
BDNF Acts Through the TrkB Receptor Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a key growth factor for neurons. It binds the TrkB receptor (tropomyosin receptor kinase B), driving neuron survival, growth, and synaptic plasticity — the cellular basis of learning and memory.
BDNF–TrkB signaling is reduced in depression and chronic stress, and antidepressants (and ketamine) raise BDNF — the “neurotrophic” theory of how they work.
Real-world hook: BDNF = fertilizer for neurons, acting through TrkB; low BDNF links to depression, and raising it aids recovery.

Because it acts as both an inducer and substrate of CYP3A4, which of the following medications might require a dose increase after several weeks to maintain steady-state blood levels?
explanation_text:
Carbamazepine: Autoinduction Carbamazepine is both a substrate AND an inducer of CYP3A4. Over the first few weeks it ramps up the very enzymes that break it down (autoinduction), so its own blood level falls over time.
That is why a dose that worked initially often needs to be increased after 2–4 weeks to keep a steady therapeutic level. It also speeds metabolism of many other drugs (oral contraceptives, lamotrigine).
Real-world hook: carbamazepine “eats itself” — recheck levels and expect to dose up early in treatment.

An elderly male has been on longstanding antiepileptic medication. Recently, he has had a fall without detected fracture, and a bone scan reveals low bone density. Which of the following medications should be avoided to prevent further bone loss?
explanation_text:
Antiepileptics and Bone Loss Long-term enzyme-affecting antiepileptics (valproate here, also carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) speed up vitamin D metabolism, which lowers calcium absorption and causes osteoporosis and fractures over time.
In an older patient with low bone density and a fall, move away from the bone-unfriendly agent and add vitamin D, calcium, and bone monitoring; newer drugs like levetiracetam are gentler on bone.
Real-world hook: chronic seizure meds quietly weaken bones through vitamin D — check bone density and supplement.

explanation_text:
Dissociative Amnesia: Autobiographical Memory Dissociative amnesia is the inability to recall important personal information — usually around trauma or stress — that is too extensive to be ordinary forgetting. The lost memory is autobiographical (episodic memories of one’s own life); facts, skills, and general knowledge stay intact.
It is psychogenic, not caused by brain injury or substances, and memory often returns later.
Real-world hook: forgets a chunk of their own life after stress but can still read, drive, and recall facts = dissociative (autobiographical) amnesia.

The relative intensity of DNA transcription activity is best determined by which of the following?
explanation_text:
Epigenetics: Histone Acetylation Opens DNA DNA is wound around histones. Histone acetylation loosens that packaging, opening the chromatin so transcription machinery can reach the genes — so acetylation = more transcription. Deacetylation tightens it and silences genes.
This is a key epigenetic switch (alongside DNA methylation, which generally silences genes); it changes gene expression without changing the DNA sequence.
Real-world hook: acetylation = “open/active” DNA; methylation = “closed/silenced.” Relevant to mood disorders, addiction, and HDAC-inhibitor drugs.

stem: When a patient in alcohol withdrawal is experiencing hallucinations, the presence of which of the following would suggest a diagnosis of alcohol hallucinosis rather than delirium tremens?
explanation_text:
Alcohol Hallucinosis vs. Delirium Tremens Both occur in alcohol withdrawal, but the key difference is the sensorium (level of consciousness and orientation). Alcohol hallucinosis = hallucinations with a CLEAR sensorium — the patient is alert, oriented, and otherwise stable.
Delirium tremens is a medical emergency: clouded consciousness, disorientation, autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, hypertension), and high mortality.
Real-world hook: clear and oriented but hallucinating = hallucinosis; confused with unstable vitals = DTs, which you treat aggressively.

A 17-year-old patient is brought to the emergency room by the father for medical evaluation following a fight with several teammates during soccer practice. According to the father, the patient often "talks back" to the coach, engages in physical fights with other members of the team, and has received detention for bullying classmates on social media and stealing a classmate's phone during lunch. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Conduct Disorder vs. ODD vs. Antisocial PD Conduct disorder = a repetitive pattern of violating others’ rights and major social norms in someone under 18: aggression toward people or animals, theft, deceit, destruction, serious rule-breaking. Fighting, bullying, and stealing fit this.
Oppositional defiant disorder is milder — arguing, defiance, irritability without serious violations. Antisocial personality disorder is the same pattern but requires age 18+ (with conduct disorder before 15).
Real-world hook: under-18 + violating others’ rights (aggression, theft) = conduct disorder; the adult version is antisocial personality disorder.

Which of the following concomitant medications would warrant a lower starting and target dose of lamotrigine?
explanation_text:
Lamotrigine + Valproate: Go Low and Slow Valproate inhibits lamotrigine’s metabolism, roughly doubling its blood level. Higher lamotrigine levels and fast titration raise the risk of the dangerous rash Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
So when adding lamotrigine to valproate, use a lower starting dose, slower titration, and a lower target. The opposite is true for enzyme inducers like carbamazepine, which lower lamotrigine levels and need higher doses.
Real-world hook: lamotrigine + valproate = halve the dose and titrate slowly to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

By raw numbers white men account for the most deaths, but the per-capita rate is highest among Native Americans.

The patient is decisionally capable, despite her distress, and the psychiatrist feels great empathy for her. In this example, which two ethical principles are in opposition?
explanation_text:
Four Principles: Autonomy vs. Nonmaleficence The four medical-ethics principles: autonomy (respect the patient’s choices), beneficence (do good), nonmaleficence (do no harm), and justice (fairness). Here the capable patient’s wish to die (autonomy) clashes with the duty not to facilitate harm or death (nonmaleficence).
The tip-off: she is decisionally capable, so autonomy carries weight, yet helping her die conflicts with “do no harm.” That tension defines the case.
Real-world hook: a patient wants something that could harm them = autonomy vs nonmaleficence.
