explanation_text:
Answer: E — Ventromedial prefrontal cortex Why E: In PTSD, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex — which normally regulates/inhibits the amygdala — is HYPOresponsive (underactive), while the amygdala is HYPERresponsive. This failure of top-down fear regulation drives the exaggerated threat response.

Why not the others:
Not A, Insula — typically HYPERactive in PTSD (threat/interoception).
Not B, Amygdala — HYPERresponsive in PTSD, not hypo.
Not C, Hippocampus — shows reduced volume/dysfunction, but the question targets the hyporesponsive regulatory region (vmPFC).
Not D, Anterior paralimbic cortex — not the classic hyporesponsive region here.

stem: Which of the following abnormalities of speech or language is a patient with autism spectrum disorder most likely to demonstrate?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Impaired prosody Why C: In autism spectrum disorder, grammar may be intact but PROSODY (the rhythm, melody, stress, and intonation of speech) is impaired — producing flat, monotone, or sing-song speech with reduced emotional expression.

Why not the others:
Not A, Dyslexia — a reading disorder, not the core ASD speech feature.
Not B, Aphasia — language loss from focal brain injury, not ASD.
Not D, Pressured speech — rapid, hard-to-interrupt speech of mania, not ASD.
Not E, Problematic enunciation — an articulation issue; ASD’s hallmark is prosody, not articulation.

stem: Following a sore throat, a child develops uncontrolled movement disorder characterized by writhing movements of the limbs and head turning. This condition has been associated with which of the following organisms?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Streptococcus Why C: This is Sydenham chorea — a post-streptococcal autoimmune complication (a major criterion of rheumatic fever). After Group A Streptococcus infection, cross-reactive antibodies attack the basal ganglia, producing chorea (writhing movements).

Why not the others:
Not A, Pseudomonas — not linked to chorea.
Not B, Mycoplasma — causes atypical pneumonia/other neuro issues, but not Sydenham chorea.
Not D, Adenovirus — not associated with chorea.
Not E, Clostridium botulinum — causes flaccid paralysis (botulism), the opposite picture.

stem: Which of the following best describes a characteristic of the implicit memory system?

options.text: Matures fully at approximately two years of age
Activates during a subjective sense of "remembering"
Consists of mental models that summate multiple experiences
Utilizes circuits primarily based in the hippocampus and orbitofrontal cortex

answer_text: Consists of mental models that summate multiple experiences
answer_raw: D. Consists of mental models that summate multiple experiences
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Consists of mental models that summate multiple experiences Why D: Implicit (nondeclarative) memory works without conscious awareness and builds up generalized mental models from many repeated experiences (schemas, conditioned responses, skills) — not single recalled events.

Why not the others (these describe EXPLICIT/declarative memory):
Not A, Requires focal attention and awareness — implicit memory is automatic; no awareness needed.
Not B, Matures fully at ~2 years — implicit memory is present from early infancy; it’s declarative memory that matures later.
Not C, Activates during a sense of “remembering” — that conscious recollection is explicit episodic memory.
Not E, Circuits in hippocampus and orbitofrontal cortex — that’s the declarative system; implicit relies on the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and amygdala.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is hospitalized for altered mental status. The patient is having trouble staying awake or attending to conversations about her status. The medical team is concerned for brain metastasis, but when asked to consent to an MRI, the patient just repeats "Don't know, don't know." A psychiatrist is consulted to perform a capacity assessment, and determines that the patient is delirious and does not currently have capacity to make medical decisions. What should the psychiatrist tell the primary team?

options.text: Pursue a court order to obtain the MRI
Check to see if patient has an advance health care directive
Meet with the patient's family to come to a consensus regarding the treatment plan
Apply for guardianship, which must be granted before testing or treatment can proceed

answer_text: Check to see if patient has an advance health care directive
answer_raw: C. Check to see if patient has an advance health care directive
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Check for an advance health care directive Why C: When a patient lacks decision-making capacity, the first step is to look for an advance health care directive (or a designated healthcare proxy) stating the patient’s wishes or naming a surrogate — the least restrictive, patient-centered option before courts or guardianship.

Why not the others:
Not A, Proceed with the MRI — not without consent/surrogate (outside a true emergency).
Not B, Court order — overly aggressive; reserved for disputes with no directive/surrogate.
Not D, Family consensus — reasonable, but first check for an existing directive/proxy that legally governs.
Not E, Guardianship — slow and a last resort; unnecessary if a directive or surrogate exists.

stem: Which of the following is the most important physiological cause of low sexual desire in post menopausal women?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Reduced testosterone Why C: Testosterone (in women, from the ovaries and adrenals) is the main driver of LIBIDO. After menopause, declining testosterone is the most important physiological cause of reduced sexual desire.

Why not the others:
Not A, Reduced cortisol — not a determinant of libido.
Not B, Reduced estrogen — falls at menopause and causes vaginal dryness/dyspareunia, but desire is driven more by testosterone.
Not D, Increased progesterone — progesterone falls after menopause, it doesn’t rise.
Not E, Increased DHEA — adrenal androgens (DHEA) decline with age, not increase.

stem: The orexin neurons, involved in the sleep-wake cycle, are located in which of the following brain regions?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Lateral hypothalamic nuclei Why D: Orexin (hypocretin) neurons are located in the LATERAL hypothalamus. They promote wakefulness and stabilize the sleep-wake switch; their loss causes narcolepsy.

Why not the others:
Not A, Dorsal raphe — serotonergic arousal center, not the orexin source.
Not B, Ventral tegmental area — dopaminergic reward.
Not C, Tuberomammillary nucleus — histaminergic wake-promoting (downstream of orexin), not its source.
Not E, Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus — the sleep-promoting (GABA) center, the opposite function.

stem: Which of the following was the most likely cause of increased incarceration rates in the United States between the 1980s and the 2010s?

options.text: Mandatory minimum sentences for drug related offenses

answer_text: Mandatory minimum sentences for drug related offenses
answer_raw: E. Mandatory minimum sentences for drug related offenses
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Mandatory minimum sentences for drug-related offenses Why E: The dramatic US incarceration rise from the 1980s–2010s is primarily attributed to the “War on Drugs” and MANDATORY MINIMUM sentencing for drug offenses, which sharply increased prison populations.

Why not the others:
Not A, Income inequality — a contributing social factor, not the primary driver.
Not B, Firearm access — not the main cause of rising incarceration.
Not C, Illegal immigration — not the primary cause.
Not D, Deinstitutionalization — it did shift some mentally ill people into jails (“transinstitutionalization”), but the dominant driver of the surge was drug-sentencing policy.

stem: Which of the following characteristics of sleep occurs in late life?
answer_raw: C. Decreased rapid eye movement sleep
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Decreased rapid eye movement sleep Why C: With aging, sleep architecture shifts: decreased REM, decreased slow-wave (Stage ¾) sleep, more light (Stage ½) sleep, more frequent awakenings, and reduced total sleep time.

Why not the others:
Not A, Less frequent arousals — older adults have MORE frequent arousals.
Not B, Increased total sleep time — total sleep time DECREASES.
Not D, Increased Stage 4 sleep — deep slow-wave (Stage 4) DECREASES with age.
Not E, Decreased Stage 2 — Stage 2 (light sleep) proportionally INCREASES.

stem: A 22-year-old man has a history of episodic severe headaches, characterized by severe pain behind the eye, abrupt onset, and duration of one hour, accompanied by conjunctival injection. Previously the headaches occurred a few times per year, but they are now occurring with increased frequency, with headache free periods of only one week. Which of the following would be most effective in preventing the headaches?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Verapamil Why B: This is cluster headache (severe unilateral retro-orbital pain with autonomic features like conjunctival injection, occurring in clusters). Verapamil (a calcium channel blocker) is the first-line PREVENTIVE treatment.

Why not the others:
Not A, Ibuprofen — an NSAID; not effective prevention (acute cluster treatment is high-flow oxygen and triptans).
Not C, Prednisone — useful as a short bridging prophylaxis, but verapamil is the first-line maintenance preventive.
Not D, Gabapentin — not first-line for cluster prevention.
Not E, Amitriptyline — used for tension/migraine prophylaxis, not cluster headache.

stem: Amongst psychiatric disorders measured in the Global Burden of Disease study series, which of the following has the highest measurement of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs)?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Depressive disorders Why D: Depressive disorders carry the highest disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) among psychiatric disorders in the Global Burden of Disease studies — a result of their high prevalence combined with disabling impact.

Why not the others:
Not A, Anxiety disorders — high burden, but below depression.
Not B, Drug use disorders — significant, but lower DALYs than depression.
Not C, Alcohol use disorder — substantial, but below depression.
Not E, Neurocognitive disorders — important, but not the top psychiatric DALY contributor.

stem: A rating instrument is said to have high reliability when which of the following properties is demonstrated?

options.text: Ratings are similar among different raters

answer_text: Ratings are similar among different raters
answer_raw: D. Ratings are similar among different raters
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Ratings are similar among different raters Why D: Reliability means consistency/reproducibility. High reliability shows up as SIMILAR ratings across different raters (inter-rater reliability) or across time — consistent results regardless of who is rating.

Why not the others (these describe VALIDITY):
Not A, Conform to true values — accuracy vs. truth is validity.
Not B, Precise and accurate — accuracy is validity; reliability is about consistency.
Not C, Procedures well validated — that’s validation/validity.
Not E, Accurately measure natural categories — measuring the true construct is validity.

stem: Which of the following is first-line therapy for seasonal affective disorder?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Bright light therapy Why D: Bright light therapy (about 10,000 lux in the morning) is the established first-line treatment for seasonal affective disorder — it mimics sunlight to correct the seasonal circadian/serotonergic disruption.

Why not the others:
Not A, Exercise — a helpful adjunct, not first-line.
Not B, Melatonin — limited role; not first-line.
Not C, Fluoxetine — SSRIs help (and bupropion XL is FDA-approved for prevention), but light therapy is the classic first-line.
Not E, Cognitive behavioral therapy — CBT-SAD is effective, but bright light is the established first-line.

stem: The acute stroke demonstrated in the axial MRI below would typically result in:
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Leg weakness Why D: Leg-predominant weakness points to an anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stroke. The ACA supplies the medial motor/sensory cortex — the leg/foot region of the homunculus — so an ACA infarct causes contralateral LEG weakness.

Why not the others:
Not A, aphasia — a left middle cerebral artery (language) stroke.
Not B, hearing loss — auditory cortex is bilaterally represented; stroke rarely causes isolated hearing loss.
Not C, double vision — brainstem/cranial-nerve (posterior circulation) involvement.
Not E, hemifield visual loss — a posterior cerebral artery (occipital) stroke.

stem: A patient believes the television is sending special messages intended just for the patient. Which of the following terms best describes this symptom?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Delusion of reference Why B: A delusion of reference is the belief that neutral external events (TV broadcasts, songs, strangers) carry special personal meaning directed at oneself. “The TV is sending me messages” is the classic example.

Why not the others:
Not A, Thought broadcasting — belief that one’s thoughts are transmitted/audible to others.
Not C, Thought withdrawal — belief that thoughts are being removed from one’s mind.
Not D, Delusion of control — belief that an outside force controls one’s actions/feelings (passivity).
Not E, Thought insertion — belief that thoughts are placed into one’s mind by an external force.

stem: Which of the following brain structures is the primary pacemaker for generating circadian rhythms of sleep and wakefulness in humans?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Suprachiasmatic nucleus Why E: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the master circadian pacemaker. It receives light input directly from the retina and drives daily rhythms of sleep-wake, hormone release, and body temperature.

Why not the others:
Not A, Pineal gland — secretes melatonin (an OUTPUT of the clock), but the SCN is the pacemaker that drives it.
Not B, Dentate nucleus — a cerebellar (motor) nucleus, unrelated.
Not C, Arcuate nucleus — appetite regulation, not circadian timing.
Not D, Ventromedial nucleus — a satiety center, not circadian.

stem: Which of the following hormones is diffused after synthesis, rather than being released from vesicles?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) Why C: DHEA is a STEROID hormone. Steroids are lipophilic, made on demand from cholesterol, and DIFFUSE directly across the cell membrane — they are not stored in or released from vesicles.

Why not the others (peptide/protein hormones stored in vesicles and released by exocytosis):
Not A, β-endorphin — a peptide, vesicle-released.
Not B, Luteinizing hormone — a glycoprotein, vesicle-released.
Not D, Follicle-stimulating hormone — a glycoprotein, vesicle-released.
Not E, ACTH — a peptide, vesicle-released.

stem: Which of the following culture bound syndromes is most closely related to the historical diagnosis of neurasthenia?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Shenjing Shuairuo Why D: Shenjing shuairuo (Chinese; “weakness of nerves”) is the culture-bound syndrome most closely tied to the historical diagnosis of neurasthenia — fatigue, weakness, headaches, poor concentration, and somatic complaints.

Why not the others:
Not A, Koro — fear that the genitals are retracting into the body (Southeast Asia).
Not B, Latah — an exaggerated startle with echolalia/echopraxia (Malaysia/Indonesia).
Not C, Hwa-byung — Korean “anger syndrome” from suppressed anger.
Not E, Ataque de nervios — a Latino syndrome of acute distress (shouting, crying, fainting) after a stressor.

stem: Which of the following strategies might be helpful to mitigate risk of liability to a psychiatrist involved in collaborative care?

options.text: Recognize that each state interprets mental health laws uniformly.
Limit practice to formal consultations and refrain from curbside care.
Ensure policies to address behavioral health emergencies are in place.
Assume supervisory responsibility for licensed therapists and clinicians.
Provide cross-coverage in the event the primary care physician is away.

answer_text: Ensure policies to address behavioral health emergencies are in place
answer_raw: C. Ensure policies to address behavioral health emergencies are in place.
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Ensure policies to address behavioral health emergencies are in place Why C: In collaborative care, having clear policies/protocols for behavioral health emergencies reduces the psychiatrist’s liability by defining responsibilities and ensuring safe escalation pathways.

Why not the others:
Not A, States interpret laws uniformly — false; mental-health laws vary by state, so this assumption raises risk.
Not B, Limit to formal consultations / refrain from curbside — informal consults happen; the protective step is documentation/policies, not avoiding all such care.
Not D, Assume supervisory responsibility for therapists — increases liability (vicarious responsibility), not mitigates it.
Not E, Provide cross-coverage when the PCP is away — expands duties/exposure, not a risk-mitigation strategy.

stem: By which of the following stages of development does the peer group first become an important mediator of aggression, especially in vulnerable males?
answer_raw: C. Late School Age (10 years old)
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Late School Age (10 years old) Why C: By late school age (~10 years), the peer group first becomes an important mediator of aggression, especially in vulnerable boys — peer influence, status, and group dynamics increasingly shape aggressive behavior.

Why not the others:
Not A, Preschool (4) — aggression exists but is mediated by family/temperament, not peer groups.
Not B, Early school age (7) — peers matter, but the peer group isn’t yet the key mediator of aggression.
Not D, Early adolescence (13) — peers are very influential, but peer-mediated aggression first emerges earlier (late school age).
Not E, Late adolescence (16) — later than the first emergence.

stem: Which of the following is the most specific laboratory test for identifying heavy alcohol consumption?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT) Why E: Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT) is the most SPECIFIC blood marker for sustained heavy alcohol use — it rises with chronic heavy drinking and is more specific than liver enzymes.

Why not the others:
Not A, Lipase — a pancreatic enzyme (pancreatitis), not specific to alcohol use.
Not B, Bilirubin — reflects liver dysfunction/hemolysis; nonspecific.
Not C, Prothrombin time — reflects liver synthetic function; nonspecific.
Not D, AST — raised in alcohol use (AST:ALT > 2 is suggestive) but less specific than CDT; GGT is sensitive but also nonspecific.

stem: Which of the following best describes a collaborative care team approach for people with physical and behavioral health conditions?

options.text: Medical consultants available on a psychiatric inpatient unit
Psychiatrists practicing in a health system that employs multiple other specialties
Addictive and mental health services offered within the same organization by different clinicians
Psychiatric consultants available through telepsychiatry to rural community mental health clinics
Psychiatric consultant advising the primary care team on patients who are not showing clinical improvement

answer_text: Psychiatric consultant advising the primary care team on patients who are not showing clinical improvement
answer_raw: E. Psychiatric consultant advising the primary care team on patients who are not showing clinical improvement
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Psychiatric consultant advising the primary care team on patients not improving Why E: In the evidence-based collaborative care model, a psychiatric consultant advises the primary care team — especially on patients who aren’t improving — using a registry and measurement-based, stepped care. The psychiatrist supports the PCP rather than seeing every patient.

Why not the others:
Not A, Medical consultants on a psych inpatient unit — inpatient consultation, not collaborative care in primary care.
Not B, Psychiatrists in a multi-specialty system — co-location, not the collaborative care model.
Not C, Addiction and mental health in one organization by different clinicians — integrated services, but not the defined collaborative care team.
Not D, Telepsychiatry consults to rural clinics — a telehealth access model, not the registry/stepped-care collaborative model.

stem: A patient is being transitioned from olanzapine to ziprasidone due to rapid development of dyslipidemia and weight gain. To avoid lowering the oral absorption of ziprasidone by 50%, the patient is counseled to take the medication:

options.text: with at least eight ounces of water.
with a high carbohydrate content meal.
with a caloric intake of at least 500 calories.

answer_text: with a caloric intake of at least 500 calories
answer_raw: E. with a caloric intake of at least 500 calories.
explanation_text:
Answer: E — With a caloric intake of at least 500 calories Why E: Ziprasidone’s oral absorption roughly DOUBLES when taken with food — specifically a meal of at least ~500 calories. On an empty stomach, absorption drops by about half, reducing efficacy, so counsel patients to take it with a substantial (≥500 kcal) meal.

Why not the others:
Not A, while fasting — fasting LOWERS absorption (the problem to avoid).
Not B, low-fat meal — it’s the caloric content (~500 kcal), not fat content, that matters.
Not C, eight ounces of water — water doesn’t drive the food effect.
Not D, high-carbohydrate meal — it’s total calories, not carbohydrate content specifically.

stem: An elderly patient with memory impairment and gait disturbance is being evaluated in a neurology clinic. After a large-volume lumbar puncture, his gait is noted to improve, thus a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is scheduled. What gait would be typical for the presumed diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Magnetic Why D: This is normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) — the triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and dementia (“wet, wobbly, wacky”). The classic gait is MAGNETIC: feet appear stuck to the floor, broad-based and shuffling. Improvement after a large-volume LP predicts shunt response.

Why not the others:
Not A, Scissor — spastic leg adduction (e.g., cerebral palsy/cord lesion), not NPH.
Not B, Spastic — stiff, circumducting gait of UMN lesions, not the NPH magnetic gait.
Not C, Tandem — a coordination test, not a disease-specific gait.
Not E, Propulsive — the festinating, stooped gait of Parkinson’s, not NPH.

stem: Which of the following prevents health insurance issuers from imposing more restrictive benefit limitations on behavioral health benefits than on medical benefits?

options.text: Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act
Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act

answer_text: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
answer_raw: E. Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act Why E: The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) prohibits health plans from imposing more restrictive limits (copays, visit limits, treatment limits) on mental health/substance use benefits than on medical/surgical benefits.

Why not the others:
Not A, Stark Law — bans physician self-referral (financial conflicts), unrelated to parity.
Not B, Uniform Commercial Code — governs commercial transactions, unrelated.
Not C, Healthcare Quality Improvement Act — protects peer review/credentialing, not parity.
Not D, EMTALA — requires emergency screening/stabilization regardless of ability to pay, not parity.

stem: The physiologic changes during REM sleep include increased eye movements, decreased muscle tone and which of the following?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Increased heart rate Why A: REM is physiologically activated (“paradoxical sleep”): increased and variable heart rate, increased/irregular respirations, raised blood pressure, increased cerebral blood flow, and genital engorgement — alongside the eye movements and muscle atonia.

Why not the others:
Not B, Increased muscle activity — REM has muscle ATONIA (paralysis), the opposite.
Not C, Decreased blood pressure — BP increases/fluctuates in REM.
Not D, Decreased respirations — respirations increase and become irregular.
Not E, Decreased cerebral blood flow — cerebral blood flow INCREASES in REM.

stem: Broad face, flat midface, progressively coarsening facial features, short, broad hands, small toes, and hoarse, deep voice, are physical features associated with the chromosomal deletion of:
explanation_text:
Answer: D — 17p11.2 (Smith-Magenis syndrome) Why D: This describes Smith-Magenis syndrome, caused by a 17p11.2 deletion — broad/flat midface, coarsening features, short broad hands, small toes, hoarse deep voice, intellectual disability, marked sleep disturbance, and self-injurious behavior.

Why not the others (other deletion syndromes):
Not A, 2q9-12 — not a recognized classic syndrome here.
Not B, 5p15.2 — Cri-du-chat syndrome (high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly).
Not C, 7q11-23 — Williams syndrome (elfin face, very sociable, supravalvular aortic stenosis).
Not E, 22q11 — DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome (cardiac defects, cleft palate, hypocalcemia, immune problems).

stem: Compared to magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography of which of the following areas is typically limited due to imaging artifacts?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Posterior fossa Why D: The posterior fossa (brainstem, cerebellum) is encased in dense bone, which produces beam-hardening/streak artifacts on CT and degrades image quality there. MRI is far superior for the posterior fossa.

Why not the others (CT performs well here):
Not A, Orbits — CT images the orbits well (fractures, foreign bodies).
Not B, Inner ear — high-resolution temporal-bone CT is excellent.
Not C, Frontal sinuses — CT is the modality of choice for sinuses.
Not E, Lumbar spinal cord — MRI is preferred for cord detail, but it’s the bone-encased posterior fossa that is classically CT-artifact-limited.

stem: Disorders such as pathological gambling and opioid use disorder are perpetuated via activation of the pathway connecting the nucleus accumbens and which of the following?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Ventral tegmental area Why D: Addictive disorders (including behavioral addictions like gambling) are perpetuated by the mesolimbic reward pathway connecting the ventral tegmental area (VTA, the dopamine source) to the nucleus accumbens.

Why not the others:
Not A, Hippocampus — memory/context, not the reward pathway terminal.
Not B, Dorsal striatum — involved in later habit formation, but the core reward circuit is VTA→accumbens.
Not C, Orbitofrontal cortex — value/decision-making, not the source projecting to the accumbens.
Not E, Anterior cingulate cortex — salience/conflict monitoring, not the dopaminergic source.

stem: Which of the following is an expected side effect that can occur with activation of a vagal nerve stimulator?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Dyspnea Why A: The vagus nerve also supplies the larynx/airway, so vagal nerve stimulator activation commonly causes voice alteration/hoarseness, cough, throat tightness, and DYSPNEA (shortness of breath) during the stimulation cycles.

Why not the others (not VNS effects):
Not B, Hand tremor — not caused by VNS.
Not C, Arm weakness — not caused by VNS.
Not D, Dysconjugate gaze — not caused by VNS.
Not E, Loss of consciousness — not an expected VNS side effect.

stem: During a session the psychiatrist tells a long-time patient, "I am moving to another state and will not be able to see you anymore. This is our last session. I am giving you a one-month supply of medication. Here is a letter documenting the end of our treatment relationship: please sign here to acknowledge it. This concludes our session." The patient independently finds another psychiatrist and establishes care without incident. Three months later, the patient sues the previous psychiatrist for damages, citing abandonment. Which of the following is the best defense against medical malpractice?

options.text: Patient did not suffer an appreciably bad outcome.
Patient filed outside the time period of the statute of limitations.
Psychiatrist now lives in another state and is not liable for prior activities.
Psychiatrist fulfilled the duty to the patient by giving 30 days of medication.
Psychiatrist provided written notification of termination that the patient signed.

answer_text: Patient did not suffer an appreciably bad outcome
answer_raw: A. Patient did not suffer an appreciably bad outcome.
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Patient did not suffer an appreciably bad outcome Why A: Malpractice requires all four elements (Duty, Dereliction, Damages, Direct causation). Here the patient found new care without incident — so there were no DAMAGES. No demonstrable harm is the strongest defense, since malpractice can’t be proven without it.

Why not the others:
Not B, Filed outside the statute of limitations — only 3 months passed; the claim is timely.
Not C, Psychiatrist now lives elsewhere — relocation doesn’t shield liability for prior care.
Not D, Gave 30 days of medication — abrupt termination may still be improper; the real defense is the absence of harm.
Not E, Written termination the patient signed — documentation helps, but the decisive defense is no damages.

stem: A student attributes poor performance on his surgery rotation to the observation that the attending does not like him and the surgical techs are always "in his way". This type of psychodynamic defense mechanism is known as:
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Rationalization Why C: Rationalization is justifying a failure with plausible but false explanations. Blaming his poor performance on the attending “not liking him” and the techs being “in his way” rationalizes away his own responsibility.

Why not the others:
Not A, denial — refusing to acknowledge reality; he admits the poor performance, just misattributes the cause.
Not B, sublimation — channeling unacceptable impulses into productive activity (a mature defense).
Not D, isolation of affect — separating emotion from the facts of an event.
Not E, reaction formation — behaving the opposite of one’s true feelings.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents for follow up after bariatric surgery. Four weeks after surgery, she developed vertigo and headache. A family member reports that she has been confused for the past week. Physical exam reveals restricted eye movements on lateral gaze. Which of the following treatments is indicated for her condition?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Thiamine Why C: This is Wernicke encephalopathy — the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia (restricted lateral gaze), and ataxia — here after bariatric surgery, a cause of thiamine deficiency. Urgent IV THIAMINE is the treatment, given BEFORE glucose.

Why not the others:
Not A, Copper — deficiency causes a myelopathy/neuropathy after bariatric surgery, not this acute Wernicke triad.
Not B, Glucose — giving glucose first (without thiamine) can precipitate/worsen Wernicke; thiamine must come first.
Not D, Solumedrol (steroid) — not the treatment for Wernicke.
Not E, Carbamazepine — an anticonvulsant; not indicated here.

stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department by family members who report that the patient has a history of depression and has recently been complaining of hearing voices. Two days ago, the patient stopped speaking and began maintaining unusual postures for hours at a time. During examination the alert patient says nothing and sits without moving. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic intervention?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Lorazepam Why D: This is catatonia (mutism, posturing, immobility/stupor). A lorazepam (benzodiazepine) challenge is first-line and can rapidly relieve catatonic symptoms; ECT is used if benzodiazepines fail.

Why not the others:
Not A, Haloperidol — high-potency antipsychotics can WORSEN catatonia and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome/malignant catatonia.
Not B, Olanzapine — also an antipsychotic; not first-line and may worsen catatonia.
Not C, Fluoxetine — an antidepressant; not the acute catatonia treatment.
Not E, Methylphenidate — a stimulant; not indicated for catatonia.

stem: In adult brains, neurogenesis occurs in the olfactory bulb and in which other of the following neural structures?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Hippocampus Why D: In adults, neurogenesis (new neuron formation) occurs at two main sites: the olfactory bulb (from the subventricular zone) and the HIPPOCAMPUS (the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus).

Why not the others (no significant adult neurogenesis):
Not A, Pons — no significant adult neurogenesis.
Not B, Thalamus — no significant adult neurogenesis.
Not C, Basal ganglia — not an established adult neurogenesis site.
Not E, Prefrontal cortex — neocortex generally doesn’t undergo significant adult neurogenesis.

stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters is released from cerebellar Purkinje cells to deeper cerebellar nuclei?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — GABA Why A: Cerebellar Purkinje cells are GABAergic — they release GABA (inhibitory) onto the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, and that output is inhibitory.

Why not the others:
Not B, Serotonin — from the raphe nuclei.
Not C, Dopamine — from the substantia nigra/VTA.
Not D, Glutamate — excitatory (granule/mossy/climbing fibers), but Purkinje OUTPUT is inhibitory GABA.
Not E, Acetylcholine — from basal forebrain/brainstem, not Purkinje cells.

stem: Which of the following hormones best facilitates the recognition of facial expression and emotion?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Oxytocin Why A: Oxytocin enhances social cognition — it improves recognition of facial expressions and emotions and promotes trust/bonding.

Why not the others:
Not B, Prolactin — lactation/parental behavior, not facial-emotion recognition.
Not C, Estrogen — affects mood/cognition broadly, but not this specific role.
Not D, Epinephrine — fight-or-flight arousal, not social cognition.
Not E, Testosterone — tends to REDUCE empathic/facial-emotion sensitivity, opposite of oxytocin.

stem: A 14-month-old child spends time with the mother in a playroom, then a stranger joins them. The mother leaves the room, returns, then both the mother and stranger exit the room together. After a short time, the mother reunites with the child in the room. Which of the following behaviors would the child most likely demonstrate assuming a secure attachment?

options.text: Both clinging to and hitting the mother upon return
Minimal reaction when the mother leaves and returns
Upset when the mother leaves, and calms with her return
Calm when the mother leaves, and upset when she returns
Upset when the mother leaves, and remains upset when she returns

answer_text: Upset when the mother leaves, and calms with her return
answer_raw: C. Upset when the mother leaves, and calms with her return
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Upset when the mother leaves, and calms with her return Why C: In Ainsworth’s Strange Situation, a SECURELY attached child shows distress when the caregiver leaves but is readily comforted and calms on reunion — using the caregiver as a secure base.

Why not the others:
Not A, Clinging and hitting on return — anxious-resistant/ambivalent (or disorganized) attachment.
Not B, Minimal reaction to leaving/returning — avoidant attachment.
Not D, Calm when she leaves, upset when she returns — an atypical/disorganized pattern.
Not E, Upset and remains inconsolable on return — anxious-resistant/ambivalent attachment.

stem: In community-dwelling older adults, greater spirituality is associated with higher:
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Resilience Why B: In community-dwelling older adults, greater spirituality is associated with higher RESILIENCE — better coping, meaning-making, and recovery from stress.

Why not the others:
Not A, income — spirituality isn’t linked to higher income.
Not C, education — not the association.
Not D, rates of alcohol use — spirituality is linked to LOWER substance use.
Not E, rates of cognitive decline — spirituality is associated with better, not worse, outcomes.

stem: Brain imaging showing hyperactivity in a brain circuit involving orbitofrontal cortex, basal ganglia, and thalamus is seen in which of the following disorders?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Obsessive-compulsive disorder Why E: OCD is associated with hyperactivity in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop — orbitofrontal cortex, basal ganglia (caudate), and thalamus. This overactive circuit underlies obsessions/compulsions and normalizes with effective treatment (SSRIs, CBT).

Why not the others:
Not A, Panic — amygdala/brainstem fear circuits, not the OFC-striatal loop.
Not B, Acute stress — amygdala-mediated, not this circuit.
Not C, Generalized anxiety — diffuse limbic/cortical, not the OCD loop.
Not D, PTSD — amygdala hyperactivity with vmPFC hypoactivity, not the OFC-basal ganglia-thalamus loop.

stem: Which of the labelled white matter tracts in this figure is most commonly known as the uncinate fasciculus?
explanation_text:
Answer: C Why C: The uncinate fasciculus is a hook-shaped white-matter tract connecting the inferior/orbitofrontal lobe with the anterior temporal lobe (label C in this midsagittal view). It integrates emotion with memory and is implicated in social-emotional processing.

Why not the others (per the figure’s labels):
Not A — a more superior association/cingulum-region fiber.
Not B — a different association tract, not the frontotemporal hook.
Not D — points to the splenium of the corpus callosum.
Not E — points to the fornix.

stem: Which of the following basic cognitive functions most commonly affects the ability of healthy elderly adults to switch between tasks?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Attention Why A: Task-switching (set-shifting) depends heavily on ATTENTION (selective/divided attention). In healthy aging, decline in attention most commonly impairs the ability to switch between tasks.

Why not the others:
Not B, Sensory memory — a brief sensory store; not the limiting factor for switching.
Not C, Pattern recognition — relatively preserved in aging.
Not D, Executive functioning — task-switching IS an executive function, but the question asks the BASIC underlying process, which is attention.
Not E, Visuoconstructive ability — drawing/construction, not task-switching.

stem: The FDA has approved which of the following antipsychotics for augmentation of antidepressants in the treatment of major depressive disorder?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Quetiapine Why B: Quetiapine (extended-release) is FDA-approved as adjunctive/augmentation therapy for major depressive disorder, added to an antidepressant. (Aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and the olanzapine-fluoxetine combination are also approved adjuncts.)

Why not the others:
Not A, Clozapine — for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, not MDD augmentation.
Not C, Lurasidone — approved for bipolar depression and schizophrenia, not adjunctive MDD.
Not D, Ziprasidone — schizophrenia/bipolar mania, not MDD augmentation.
Not E, Risperidone — used off-label for augmentation, but not FDA-approved for adjunctive MDD.

stem: Which of the following receptors is most critical for triggering long term potentiation?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) Why A: The NMDA receptor triggers long-term potentiation (LTP). It’s a coincidence detector — it opens (allowing calcium influx) only when the postsynaptic cell is depolarized (removing its Mg2+ block) AND glutamate binds. That calcium signal initiates LTP.

Why not the others:
Not B, GABA — inhibitory; not the trigger for LTP.
Not C, TrkB — the BDNF receptor; supports plasticity but isn’t the trigger.
Not D, BDNF — a growth factor that helps maintain LTP, not trigger it.
Not E, AMPA — mediates fast excitatory transmission and is INSERTED to express LTP, but NMDA activation is what triggers it.

stem: Mirtazapine induces less nausea than many other anti-depressants due to its blockade of which of the following serotonin receptors?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — 5-HT3 Why C: Mirtazapine blocks the 5-HT3 receptor, which is why it causes LESS nausea than SSRIs/SNRIs (it can even be antiemetic and appetite-stimulating). It also blocks 5-HT2 (improved sleep, less sexual dysfunction) and H1 (sedation, weight gain).

Why not the others:
Not A, 5-HT1 — relates to mood/anxiety effects, not the antinausea mechanism.
Not B, 5-HT2 — mirtazapine blocks it (sleep/appetite), but nausea reduction is via 5-HT3.
Not D, 5-HT4 — gut motility; not the mirtazapine antinausea target.
Not E, 5-HT5 — minor role; not relevant here.

stem: Research indicates that children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and healthy controls both respond similarly to treatment with central nervous system stimulants, including increased ability to concentrate and improved executive functioning. Using this research as an argument that such medications should be available to all children to improve functioning rests mainly on which ethical principle?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Justice Why A: Justice is the ethical principle of fairness in distributing benefits and resources. Arguing that ALL children should have access to cognitive-enhancing medication appeals to fairness/equal access — justice.

Why not the others:
Not B, Veracity — truthfulness/honesty, not distribution.
Not C, Autonomy — respecting individual choice, not the equal-access argument.
Not D, Beneficence — doing good for a given patient; here the argument is fair distribution across everyone.
Not E, Nonmaleficence — avoiding harm, not the issue.

stem: Which of the labels in the figure below most correctly identifies the habenula?
explanation_text:
Answer: D Why D: The habenula is a small epithalamic structure on the dorsomedial aspect of the thalamus, beside the third ventricle (label D in this coronal section). It links the limbic system to midbrain monoaminergic nuclei and is implicated in reward/aversion and depression.

Why not the others (per the figure’s labels):
Not A — a more lateral deep gray structure (basal ganglia region).
Not B — a more inferior/medial temporal label.
Not C — an inferior temporal-region label.
Not E — an adjacent structure just off the habenula’s dorsomedial position.

stem: Which of the following is a mechanism underlying epigenetic effects on genetic expression?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — DNA methylation Why C: DNA methylation is a key epigenetic mechanism — adding methyl groups (typically at CpG sites) to silence gene expression WITHOUT changing the DNA sequence. (Histone modification and noncoding RNAs are other epigenetic mechanisms.)

Why not the others:
Not A, Mitosis — ordinary cell division, not an epigenetic gene-regulation mechanism.
Not B, Meiosis — gamete formation/recombination, not epigenetic.
Not D, Selective mutation — changes the DNA SEQUENCE (genetic, not epigenetic).
Not E, Trinucleotide repeats — a sequence-based mutation (e.g., fragile X, Huntington), not epigenetic.

stem: Which of the following parental tasks first becomes especially important during toddlerhood?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Limit setting Why C: Toddlerhood (the autonomy stage) is when LIMIT SETTING first becomes especially important — the child explores independence and needs consistent boundaries for safety and self-regulation.

Why not the others:
Not A, Attachment — the central task of INFANCY (first year), established earlier.
Not B, Nurturance — fundamental from birth, not first emerging in toddlerhood.
Not D, Stimulation — important from infancy onward, not specific to toddlerhood.
Not E, Instruction — becomes prominent later (school age), not toddlerhood.

stem: A 70-year-old patient was hospitalized because of a middle cerebral artery stroke. The psychiatrist was asked to evaluate the patient. The patient has nonfluent aphasia. Which of the following most likely characterized the patient's interaction with the psychiatrist?

options.text: The patient spoke at a normal rate.
The patient's interpretation of proverbs was concrete.
The patient was able to repeat, "no ands, ifs, or buts."
The patient was able to follow the verbal request, "Close your eyes."
The patient was able to explain to the psychiatrist why the patient was in the hospital.

answer_text: The patient was able to follow the verbal request, "Close your eyes."
answer_raw: D. The patient was able to follow the verbal request, "Close your eyes."
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Could follow “close your eyes” Why D: Nonfluent (Broca’s) aphasia = effortful, sparse speech with IMPAIRED repetition but PRESERVED comprehension. So the patient can follow a simple command (“close your eyes”) because understanding is intact.

Why not the others:
Not A, spoke at a normal rate — Broca’s is nonfluent (slow, effortful), not normal rate.
Not B, concrete proverb interpretation — reflects abstraction/executive issues, not the defining Broca feature.
Not C, able to repeat “no ands, ifs, or buts” — repetition is IMPAIRED in Broca’s aphasia.
Not E, able to explain why hospitalized — requires fluent expressive speech, which Broca’s patients lack.

stem: The behavioral and visceral responses in fear are mediated by projections to the brainstem and hypothalamic nuclei from which of the following?

options.text: The shell of the nucleus accumbens

answer_raw: E. Centromedial nuclei of the amygdala
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Centromedial nuclei of the amygdala Why E: The central/centromedial nuclei of the amygdala are the main OUTPUT, projecting to the brainstem and hypothalamus to produce the behavioral (freezing) and visceral/autonomic responses of fear.

Why not the others:
Not A, Locus ceruleus — noradrenergic arousal; receives amygdala input but isn’t the fear-output source.
Not B, Medial prefrontal cortex — regulates/inhibits the amygdala (top-down), not the output to brainstem/hypothalamus.
Not C, Dentate gyrus of the hippocampus — memory/context, not the fear-response output.
Not D, Shell of the nucleus accumbens — reward circuitry, not fear output.

stem: A therapeutic factor in group therapy in which individuals develop awareness that they are not alone in their struggles and that others share similar problems, is known as:
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Universalization Why E: Universalization (Yalom’s “universality”) is the group-therapy factor in which members realize they are NOT alone — others share similar struggles — reducing isolation and shame.

Why not the others:
Not A, cohesion — the sense of belonging/bonding in the group, not the “not alone” realization.
Not B, contagion — the spread of emotions/behaviors through the group, not therapeutic universality.
Not C, inspiration (instillation of hope) — gaining optimism from seeing others’ progress.
Not D, acceptance — feeling accepted by the group; related but distinct from recognizing shared problems.

stem: Which of the following agencies inspects hospitals every few years, sets the standards of hospital care and performance, and is involved in preventing medical errors?

options.text: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education

explanation_text:
Answer: A — Joint Commission Why A: The Joint Commission accredits and inspects hospitals (surveys roughly every 3 years), sets standards for care and safety, and drives medical-error prevention (e.g., National Patient Safety Goals).

Why not the others:
Not B, Institute of Medicine — issues influential reports (e.g., “To Err Is Human”) but doesn’t inspect/accredit hospitals.
Not C, National Quality Forum — endorses quality measures, doesn’t inspect hospitals.
Not D, CMS — administers Medicare/Medicaid and conditions of participation, but accreditation surveys are the Joint Commission’s role.
Not E, ACGME — accredits residency/graduate medical education programs, not hospitals.

stem: Which of the following demographic features is associated with persistence of symptoms in adult patients diagnosed with somatic symptom disorder?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Lower educational level Why D: Lower educational level is associated with persistence of symptoms in somatic symptom disorder (along with older age, comorbid anxiety/depression, and unemployment).

Why not the others:
Not A, Male gender — somatic symptom disorder is more common in women; male gender isn’t the persistence predictor.
Not B, Younger age — older age tends to predict persistence.
Not C, Current employment — employment is generally protective, not a persistence factor.
Not E, Higher socioeconomic status — LOWER SES is associated with persistence.

stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters has the highest affinity for the human Cannabinoid CB-1 receptor?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Anandamide Why B: Anandamide (“the bliss molecule”) is an endocannabinoid with the highest affinity for the CB-1 receptor — a high-affinity partial agonist.

Why not the others:
Not A, Virodhamine — a partial agonist/antagonist endocannabinoid with lower CB1 affinity.
Not C, 2-arachidonylglycerol (2-AG) — the most ABUNDANT endocannabinoid, but lower CB1 affinity than anandamide.
Not D, N-arachidonyldopamine — a minor endocannabinoid.
Not E, 2-arachidonoylglycerol ether (noladin ether) — a minor endocannabinoid.

stem: Referring a patient with schizophrenia to a vocational rehabilitation program best represents an example of which of the following?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Tertiary prevention Why B: Tertiary prevention reduces disability and improves functioning in people who ALREADY have an established disease. Vocational rehabilitation for schizophrenia — restoring function — is tertiary prevention.

Why not the others:
Not A, Health promotion — general wellness efforts, not disease-specific rehabilitation.
Not C, Primary prevention — preventing disease before it occurs (reducing risk factors).
Not D, Secondary prevention — early detection/screening to catch disease early.
Not E, Population-based intervention — a scope descriptor, not the prevention level here.

stem: A 25-year-old patient repeatedly presents to the emergency department endorsing vague headaches, abdominal pain, and fatigue. Repeated diagnostic tests show no clear medical etiology, but the patient expresses great anxiety about the fact that the symptoms are not being addressed. A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder should be considered because the:

options.text: patient has more than one somatic complaint.
somatic symptoms began before the age of 30.
patient is likely intentionally feigning the symptoms.
patient has excessive behaviors related to the symptoms.

answer_text: patient has excessive behaviors related to the symptoms
answer_raw: E. patient has excessive behaviors related to the symptoms.
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Excessive behaviors related to the symptoms Why E: DSM-5 defines somatic symptom disorder by the patient’s EXCESSIVE thoughts, feelings, or behaviors about the symptoms (disproportionate worry, high anxiety, excessive time/energy) — not by whether the symptoms are medically explained.

Why not the others:
Not A, symptoms medically unexplained — DSM-5 DROPPED the “medically unexplained” requirement; symptoms may or may not have a medical cause.
Not B, more than one somatic complaint — only one distressing somatic symptom is required.
Not C, began before age 30 — that was the old somatization disorder criterion, removed in DSM-5.
Not D, intentionally feigning — that’s factitious disorder/malingering; in SSD the symptoms are not intentionally produced.

stem: Postpartum psychosis is often associated with which of the following disorders?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Bipolar Why A: Postpartum psychosis is most strongly associated with BIPOLAR disorder — it’s often a manifestation of bipolar illness with high recurrence risk. It’s a psychiatric emergency (risk of harm to self and infant).

Why not the others:
Not B, Delusional disorder — not the classic association.
Not C, Schizophrenia — can have postpartum exacerbations, but bipolar is the strongest link to postpartum psychosis.
Not D, Major depressive — postpartum DEPRESSION is common, but postpartum PSYCHOSIS is most linked to bipolar.
Not E, Posttraumatic stress — not associated with postpartum psychosis.

stem: What does the term "expressed emotion" refer to in family therapy?

options.text: The level of criticism and hostility in a family
The body language family members direct at one another
The percentage of crying or laughter in a family encounter

answer_text: The level of criticism and hostility in a family
answer_raw: C. The level of criticism and hostility in a family
explanation_text:
Answer: C — The level of criticism and hostility in a family Why C: “Expressed emotion” (EE) is the level of criticism, hostility, and emotional over-involvement family members show toward a patient. HIGH EE predicts relapse in schizophrenia (and other disorders).

Why not the others:
Not A, A successful outcome — EE is a risk factor, not an outcome.
Not B, Behavioral substitutes for anger — not the definition.
Not D, Body language — EE is about critical/hostile attitudes, not nonverbal cues specifically.
Not E, Percentage of crying/laughter — not the construct.

stem: Which of the following is a method used to compute probability estimates that can allow the researcher to generalize from the sample population to the larger population from which the samples were drawn?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Confidence intervals Why C: Confidence intervals are computed from sample data to estimate the range within which the true population parameter likely falls (e.g., a 95% CI) — allowing generalization from the sample to the larger population.

Why not the others:
Not A, Odds ratios — measure strength of association, not the generalization method.
Not B, Kappa coefficient — measures inter-rater agreement.
Not D, Estimates of effect size — quantify the magnitude of an effect, not the population-inference range.
Not E, Intra-class correlation coefficient — a reliability measure.

stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters is the precursor to melatonin?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Serotonin Why B: Serotonin is the precursor to melatonin. Pathway: tryptophan → 5-HTP → serotonin → (in the pineal gland) N-acetylserotonin → melatonin.

Why not the others:
Not A, GABA — an inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitter, unrelated.
Not C, Dopamine — made from tyrosine; not a melatonin precursor.
Not D, Cholecystokinin — a gut/brain peptide, unrelated.
Not E, Norepinephrine — STIMULATES nighttime pineal melatonin synthesis, but it isn’t the chemical precursor; serotonin is the substrate.

stem: A patient presents with new onset episodes of excessive salivation, chewing and choking sensation. A seizure originating in in what area of the brain would result in these symptoms?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Frontal operculum Why B: The frontal operculum (overlying the insula, near gustatory/autonomic and orofacial motor areas) produces seizures with excessive salivation, chewing/swallowing movements, and a choking/laryngeal sensation.

Why not the others:
Not A, Frontal insula — involved in visceral/autonomic sensation, but the operculum is the classic localization for this salivation-chewing-choking cluster.
Not C, Mesial temporal lobe — epigastric rising, déjà vu, automatisms, fear — not primarily salivation/chewing.
Not D, Occipital lobe / supplementary motor area — occipital = visual phenomena; SMA = asymmetric tonic posturing.
Not E, Dorsolateral frontal / entorhinal — not the salivation/chewing localization.

stem: According to Winnicott, a caregiver who is sufficiently attuned and responsive to a child's needs to allow the child to become aware of the child's own drives is referred to as a/an:
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Good-enough parent Why E: Winnicott’s “good-enough parent (mother)” is the caregiver who is sufficiently — not perfectly — attuned and responsive, gradually allowing manageable frustration so the child becomes aware of their own drives and develops a true self.

Why not the others:
Not A, true self — the authentic self that emerges WITH good-enough parenting (a result, not the caregiver).
Not B, self object (Kohut) — a person experienced as part of/serving the self, not Winnicott’s caregiver concept.
Not C, auxiliary ego — a psychodrama term; someone who extends/acts for another’s ego.
Not D, transitional object — a comfort object (e.g., blanket) bridging self and world, not the caregiver.

stem: Which of the following disorders is most common in individuals with a family history of bipolar disorder?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Major depressive disorder Why B: Relatives of people with bipolar disorder have elevated rates of mood disorders. While bipolar risk is raised, MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER is the MOST COMMON diagnosis among them — depression is far more prevalent overall.

Why not the others:
Not A, Bipolar disorder — risk is increased, but in absolute numbers MDD is more common among relatives.
Not C, Generalized anxiety disorder — not the primary familial association.
Not D, Persistent depressive disorder — less common than MDD.
Not E, Obsessive-compulsive disorder — not the primary familial link with bipolar.

stem: Which of the following conditions has evidence of improvement using adapted models of dialectical behavior therapy?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Eating disorders Why A: Adapted DBT models have evidence for EATING DISORDERS (especially binge eating disorder and bulimia), targeting the emotion dysregulation that drives binge/purge behaviors.

Why not the others:
Not B, Anxiety disorders — CBT/exposure is first-line; DBT isn’t the evidence-based adaptation here.
Not C, Gender dysphoria — not a DBT target.
Not D, Factitious disorder — no DBT evidence base.
Not E, Paraphilic disorders — not a DBT-adapted indication.

stem: An elderly man complains of episodic blurry vision for the past three months. During the extraocular movement exam, his eyes slowly drift away from the direction of movement, followed by rapid corrections with lateral gaze. These movements do not occur when the patient is not asked to fixate on a target. These findings most strongly suggest dysfunction in the:
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Vestibular labyrinth Why C: The slow drift off-target with fast corrective saccades is a jerk nystagmus from vestibular (labyrinthine) dysfunction. The vestibular labyrinth (inner-ear semicircular canals/otoliths) supplies the signals that keep gaze stable; its dysfunction produces this nystagmus.

Why not the others:
Not A, cerebellum — causes central/gaze-evoked nystagmus and other eye-movement signs, but the labyrinth is the source here.
Not B, oculomotor nerve (CN III) — causes ptosis, a “down-and-out” eye, and diplopia, not this nystagmus.
Not D, vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) — carries the signal, but the lesion here is the labyrinth itself.
Not E, brainstem vestibular nuclei — a central cause; the keyed answer is the peripheral labyrinth.

stem: Which of the following individuals was a principal contributor to the development of object relations theory?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Melanie Klein Why B: Melanie Klein was a principal founder of object relations theory — emphasizing the infant’s internalized “objects” (mental representations of caregivers) and early splitting into good/bad (the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions).

Why not the others:
Not A, Anna Freud — ego psychology, child analysis, and defense mechanisms.
Not C, Karen Horney — feminine psychology; neurosis from social/cultural factors.
Not D, Helene Deutsch — psychology of women and the “as-if” personality.
Not E, Margaret Mahler — separation-individuation theory (related, but Klein is THE principal object-relations founder).

stem: A 25-year-old patient is hospitalized for appendicitis. Psychiatry is consulted after the patient reports to the nurse being "bothered by the surgeon's aura." The patient reports living alone, not having close friends, and enjoying frequenting websites discussing auras and crystal work. The psychiatrist speaks with the patient's mother who affirms that the patient "has always been this way." Which of the following personality disorders is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Schizotypal Why E: Schizotypal PD = odd beliefs/magical thinking (auras, crystal work), social isolation, no close friends, and lifelong (“always been this way”) — eccentric perceptual experiences without frank psychosis.

Why not the others:
Not A, Avoidant — avoids contact from fear of rejection (WANTS relationships but fears them); no magical thinking.
Not B, Borderline — unstable affect/relationships/identity and impulsivity, not odd beliefs.
Not C, Paranoid — pervasive distrust/suspiciousness, not magical thinking/auras.
Not D, Schizoid — social detachment with NO desire for relationships and NO odd beliefs (the key difference from schizotypal).

stem: Puberty begins when pulsatile secretion of gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) emanates from neurons in which of the following hypothalamic nuclei?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Infundibular (arcuate) nucleus Why B: GnRH-secreting neurons sit in the infundibular (arcuate) nucleus of the hypothalamus. At puberty their PULSATILE GnRH release drives LH/FSH secretion from the pituitary.

Why not the others:
Not A, Lateral — feeding/arousal (orexin), not GnRH.
Not C, Ventromedial — the satiety center.
Not D, Suprachiasmatic — the circadian-rhythm pacemaker.
Not E, Tuberomammillary — histaminergic, drives wakefulness.

stem: What is the psychological function of medication prescribed by a physician, when the medication serves as a transitional object for the patient?

options.text: It demonstrates the medical skill of the physician
It defends against the sense of being omnipotently controlled by the physician
It acts as a container for the patient's projected anxieties about being defective
It allows a sense of connectedness to the physician, even when visits are infrequent
It enables the patient to bridge the gap between impaired and normal ego functioning

answer_text: It allows a sense of connectedness to the physician, even when visits are infrequent
answer_raw: D. It allows a sense of connectedness to the physician, even when visits are infrequent
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Allows a sense of connectedness to the physician Why D: A transitional object provides comfort and a symbolic link. Medication as a transitional object lets the patient feel CONNECTED to the physician between visits — like a child’s blanket bridges the caregiver’s presence and absence.

Why not the others:
Not A, demonstrates medical skill — not the psychological (transitional-object) function.
Not B, defends against being omnipotently controlled — not the transitional-object concept.
Not C, container for projected anxieties — that’s Bion’s “containment,” a different idea.
Not E, bridges impaired and normal ego functioning — not the transitional-object meaning.

stem: Distressing incongruence between experienced (or expressed) gender and birth gender is labeled as which of the following?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Gender dysphoria Why B: Gender dysphoria is the DSM-5 term for clinically significant DISTRESS arising from incongruence between one’s experienced/expressed gender and birth-assigned (natal) gender. The distress is the defining feature.

Why not the others:
Not A, Depersonalization — feeling detached from oneself/unreal; unrelated to gender identity.
Not C, Transvestic disorder — sexual arousal from cross-dressing, distinct from gender-identity incongruence.
Not D, Body dysmorphic disorder — preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance, not gender identity.
Not E, Ego-dystonic sexual orientation — an outdated category about sexual orientation, not gender identity.

stem: The triple screen for Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome) measures maternal serum quantities of alpha fetoprotein, estriol, and:
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) Why D: The triple screen measures AFP, estriol (uE3), and hCG. In Down syndrome: AFP low, estriol low, hCG HIGH. (The QUAD screen adds inhibin A.)

Why not the others:
Not A, inhibin A — that’s the 4th marker in the QUAD screen, not the triple.
Not B, testosterone — not part of prenatal aneuploidy screening.
Not C, progesterone — not in the triple screen.
Not E, pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) — part of first-trimester combined screening, not the triple screen.

stem: Which of the following factors is most associated with men who assault their intimate partners?

options.text: Substance intoxication at the time of the abuse

explanation_text:
Answer: B — History of childhood abuse Why B: A history of childhood abuse — experiencing or witnessing family violence — is the factor most strongly associated with men who perpetrate intimate partner violence (the “cycle of violence”: learned, modeled behavior).

Why not the others:
Not A, Low testosterone — aggression isn’t consistently linked to low testosterone (if anything, the reverse).
Not C, Higher rates of psychotic disorders — most IPV perpetrators are not psychotic.
Not D, Elevated CSF 5-HIAA — it’s LOW 5-HIAA (low serotonin) that’s linked to impulsive aggression.
Not E, Substance intoxication at the time — a real situational trigger, but childhood abuse is the strongest underlying developmental factor.

stem: A gene can be differentially expressed after reversible gene inactivation depending on whether it was inherited from the mother or father. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Genetic imprinting Why B: Genomic (genetic) imprinting = a gene is expressed differently depending on parent of origin, via reversible epigenetic silencing (DNA methylation). Classic example: Prader-Willi (paternal deletion) vs Angelman (maternal deletion) — same region, opposite parent.

Why not the others:
Not A, Anticipation — earlier onset/worse severity across generations, not parent-of-origin silencing.
Not C, Incomplete penetrance — not everyone with the genotype shows the phenotype.
Not D, Triple repeat expansion — the mechanism behind anticipation (e.g., Huntington, fragile X), not imprinting.
Not E, X-linked recessive inheritance — an inheritance pattern, not reversible parent-of-origin inactivation.

stem: Autism spectrum disorder is most frequently associated with which of the following comorbidities?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Intellectual disability Why E: Intellectual disability is the most frequent comorbidity in autism spectrum disorder — a large share of children with ASD have co-occurring ID.

Why not the others:
Not A, Epilepsy — common (especially alongside ID), but less frequent than intellectual disability.
Not B, Depression — can co-occur (more in higher-functioning/older individuals), but not the most frequent.
Not C, Schizophrenia — not the primary comorbidity.
Not D, Selective mutism — not the most frequent ASD comorbidity.

(Note: the deck mislabels option B as “8.” — it should read “B. Depression.”)

stem: Histamine synthesis in human brain cells only occurs within which of the following areas?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Hypothalamus Why D: Brain histaminergic neurons originate exclusively in the tuberomammillary nucleus of the HYPOTHALAMUS, projecting widely to promote wakefulness/arousal.

Why not the others:
Not A, Pons — home to other monoamine nuclei (e.g., the locus ceruleus, norepinephrine), not histamine.
Not B, Medulla — autonomic centers, not histamine synthesis.
Not C, Thalamus — a sensory relay station, not the histamine source.
Not E, Cingulate cortex — limbic cortex, not a histamine-synthesizing nucleus.

stem: Which of the following symptoms is most helpful in distinguishing between epileptic and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Alertness immediately after the episode Why E: A true generalized (tonic-clonic) seizure is followed by a postictal confusional state. Rapid return to FULL alertness right after the episode points toward psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES).

Why not the others:
Not A, Head banging — can occur in either; not discriminating.
Not B, Stuttering speech — not a reliable discriminator.
Not C, Urinary incontinence — occurs in both epileptic and psychogenic events.
Not D, Injury during the episode — also occurs in both; not reliable.

stem: What type of therapy is defined as a treatment that uses direct measures to ameliorate symptoms and to maintain, restore, or improve self-esteem, ego functions, and adaptive skills?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Supportive Why A: Supportive therapy uses DIRECT measures (encouragement, reassurance, advice, environmental support) to relieve symptoms and bolster self-esteem, ego functions, and adaptive/coping skills — strengthening existing defenses rather than restructuring them.

Why not the others:
Not B, Interpersonal — time-limited; focuses on current relationships, role transitions, and grief.
Not C, Psychodynamic — explores unconscious conflicts and insight, not direct symptom support.
Not D, Cognitive-behavioral — targets maladaptive thoughts/behaviors via structured techniques.
Not E, Dialectical behavioral — skills-based (mindfulness, distress tolerance) for emotion dysregulation/BPD.

stem: Staff at psychiatric emergency services are trying to contain an agitated patient. They performed high-quality verbal de-escalation with minimal benefit. In addition to calling security for a show of force, in which of the following scenarios would it be most appropriate to place the patient in restraints?

options.text: The patient keeps approaching other patients and telling them they should cut themselves.
The patient threatens to slap family members at bedside if they share information with the evaluating team.
The patient keeps shouting that the world is a beautiful place, everything is connected, and love is everywhere.
The patient declines to participate in a clinical interview while repeatedly demanding a benzodiazepine prescription for intense anxiety.
The patient throws an object a nurse assessing him and then attempts to punch the first arriving security officer before bolting for the exit.

answer_text: The patient throws an object a nurse assessing him and then attempts to punch the first arriving security officer before bolting for the exit
answer_raw: E. The patient throws an object a nurse assessing him and then attempts to punch the first arriving security officer before bolting for the exit.
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Throws an object and attempts to punch staff while bolting Why E: Restraints are justified only for IMMINENT danger to self or others when less-restrictive measures have failed. Throwing an object at a nurse and trying to punch staff while fleeing is active physical violence — the appropriate indication.

Why not the others:
Not A, telling others to cut themselves — disturbing, but verbal; manage verbally/separate, not imminent physical danger.
Not B, threatens to slap family — a verbal threat; de-escalate first, doesn’t yet meet the imminent-danger bar.
Not C, shouting the world is beautiful/love everywhere — possibly manic but not dangerous; no restraint indication.
Not D, declines interview while demanding benzodiazepines — non-cooperative/drug-seeking, not violent.

stem: Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between estrogen and depression during the menopausal transition?

options.text: Increases in estrogen are associated with depressive episodes.
Depressive episodes occur once estrogen reaches its lowest point.
The rapidity of change in estrogen is correlated with the development of depression.
Depressive episodes are most common with high estrogen during early perimenopause.
As estrogen decreases across perimenopause, the incidence of depression increases gradually.

answer_text: The rapidity of change in estrogen is correlated with the development of depression
answer_raw: C. The rapidity of change in estrogen is correlated with the development of depression.
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Rapidity of estrogen change correlates with depression Why C: It’s the RATE/variability of estrogen change — not the absolute level — that correlates with depression risk during the menopausal transition. Rapid hormonal fluctuations in perimenopause destabilize mood.

Why not the others:
Not A, increases in estrogen cause depression — it’s fluctuation/withdrawal, not rises.
Not B, depression once estrogen is lowest — risk peaks during the transition (fluctuation), not at the stable postmenopausal low.
Not D, high estrogen in early perimenopause — not the best descriptor; variability matters more than a single level.
Not E, gradual decrease → gradual rise in depression — it’s the rapidity/variability, not a slow decline.

stem: A 61-year-old patient presents to the emergency department accompanied by family who report that the patient is unable to remember recent events. The patient's memory problems began 2 hours prior, and the patient was cognitively intact before this episode. The patient is alert, slightly anxious and frustrated, and repeatedly asks, "Why am I in the hospital, is someone sick?" This presentation is most consistent with a diagnosis of:
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Transient global amnesia Why C: Transient global amnesia = sudden, temporary anterograde amnesia (can’t form new memories) with repetitive questioning (“Why am I here?”), preserved alertness, identity, and other cognition, resolving within 24 hours. Classic in middle-aged/older adults.

Why not the others:
Not A, Korsakoff dementia — a chronic memory deficit with confabulation from thiamine deficiency, not acute/transient.
Not B, temporal lobe epilepsy — brief seizures with automatisms/altered awareness, not hours of pure amnesia with full alertness.
Not D, midline cerebellar tumor — gait ataxia/balance problems, not amnesia.
Not E, middle cerebral artery occlusion — stroke with motor/language/sensory deficits, not isolated transient amnesia.

stem: Which of the following developmental disability syndromes is associated with a triple-repeat genetic abnormality?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Fragile X syndrome Why C: Fragile X is caused by a CGG triple-repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene (X-linked). It’s the most common INHERITED cause of intellectual disability — features include a long face, large ears, macroorchidism, and autistic traits.

Why not the others:
Not A, Rett disorder — MECP2 mutation (X-linked), not a triple repeat.
Not B, Down syndrome — trisomy 21 (chromosomal nondisjunction), not a triple repeat.
Not D, Asperger disorder — no single triple-repeat genetic cause.
Not E, Williams syndrome — a microdeletion on chromosome 7 (elastin gene), not a triple repeat.

stem: A soldier in the battlefield often heard a loud shrill noise prior to nearby missile explosions. Since returning from deployment, the soldier experiences increased heart rate and respiration upon hearing a similar shrill sound. In classical conditioning, the explosions that occurred near the soldier are considered the:
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Unconditioned stimulus Why C: The explosions naturally produce fear/arousal WITHOUT learning — they are the unconditioned stimulus (UCS). The shrill noise (originally neutral) becomes the conditioned stimulus; later fear to the noise alone is the conditioned response.

Why not the others:
Not A, conditioned stimulus — that’s the shrill noise (the once-neutral cue that now triggers fear).
Not B, conditioned response — the learned fear/arousal to the shrill noise after deployment.
Not D, unconditioned response — the natural fear/arousal to the explosions (the reaction, not the stimulus).

stem: The Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression (STAR*D) trial is a pragmatic trial, designed to be more generalizable to clinical practice than standard randomized controlled trials. Which of the following aspects of STAR*D enhanced its generalizability?

options.text: It was designed to test efficacy rather than effectiveness.
The primary outcome was response rather than remission.
It incorporated patient choice into the randomization strategy.
Patients were recruited through advertising for treatment-resistant depression.

answer_text: It incorporated patient choice into the randomization strategy
answer_raw: C. It incorporated patient choice into the randomization strategy.
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Incorporated patient choice into randomization Why C: STAR*D used “equipoise-stratified randomization” — patients could decline strategies they didn’t want (e.g., switch vs augment), mirroring real-world practice and boosting generalizability.

Why not the others:
Not A, tested efficacy rather than effectiveness — reversed: STAR*D tested EFFECTIVENESS (real-world), which is what makes it generalizable.
Not B, primary outcome was response — the primary outcome was REMISSION, not response.
Not D, recruited via advertising for treatment-resistant depression — it enrolled broad real-world outpatients with MDD, not advertised TRD volunteers.

stem: Which of the following electroencephalographic findings is characteristic of a delirium of encephalopathic cause?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Increased slow wave activity Why C: Delirium from a metabolic/encephalopathic cause typically shows diffuse EEG SLOWING (increased theta/delta slow-wave activity), reflecting global cerebral dysfunction.

Why not the others:
Not A, Higher voltage activity — amplitude isn’t the characteristic finding.
Not B, Excessive fast wave activity — beta/fast activity is seen with benzodiazepine/sedative use or sedative withdrawal (e.g., delirium tremens), not typical metabolic delirium.
Not D, Increased epileptiform activity — suggests seizures, not metabolic delirium.

stem: Which of the following aspects of sleep is increased in older adults?
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Duration of awakenings Why D: With aging, nighttime awakenings increase in both number and DURATION — sleep becomes more fragmented, with more time awake after sleep onset.

Why not the others:
Not A, REM — REM sleep modestly DECREASES with age.
Not B, Slow-wave — deep slow-wave (N3) sleep DECREASES markedly with age.
Not C, Subjective quality — sleep quality generally declines, not improves.

stem: Which of the following medications have been found to be more effective than placebo in treating pain associated with diabetic neuropathy regardless if patients were depressed? (Select three)
answer_text: E. Duloxetine; G. Gabapentin; H. Venlafaxine
answer_raw: E. Duloxetine G. Gabapentin H. Venlafaxine
explanation_text:
Answer: E, G, H — Duloxetine, Gabapentin, Venlafaxine Why E, G, H: Duloxetine (SNRI), gabapentin (anticonvulsant), and venlafaxine (SNRI) all relieve diabetic neuropathic pain independent of any antidepressant effect — they act directly on pain pathways (descending inhibition; calcium-channel modulation).

Why not the others:
Not A, Sertraline / Not D, Fluoxetine — SSRIs are not effective for neuropathic pain.
Not B, Naproxen / Not C, Celecoxib — NSAIDs don’t relieve neuropathic pain.
Not F, Oxycodone — an opioid; can dull pain but isn’t first-line and carries dependence risk.
